subject: Mathematics
title: Amir and Meera's Monsoon Journey
hook: Two cousins set out on a rainy adventure across the Indian countryside — and numbers follow them everywhere.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: curious older cousin from the city

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: village girl who loves patterns and numbers

characters.name: Dadaji
characters.role: wise grandfather, keeper of stories

slides.title: We the Travellers - I
slides.storyContext: Amir arrives at his village cousins' home for the monsoon holidays. Meera greets him at the gate with a puzzled expression: she's counting raindrops falling into buckets arranged in the courtyard.

slides.title: The Monsoon Arrives
slides.storyContext: Dadaji assigns Amir and Meera a task: travel to the market to buy provisions for the week and bring back the bill. He gives them instructions written on a palm leaf, and Meera notices numbers everywhere — the cost of rice, the number of villages they must pass, the time on the old temple clock.
slides.inSimpleWords: Every journey we take, numbers guide us — the distance, the time, the money we spend.

slides.title: Numbers in Our World
slides.storyContext: At the first stop, a farmer shows them his harvest: 2,456 kg of rice he collected this season. Meera writes it down: 2,456. Amir looks confused. 'Is that really how we write it?'

points.label: Indian Place Value System
points.text: We write numbers using the Hindi place-value system: ones (ek), tens (das), hundreds (sau), thousands (hazar), ten thousands (das hazar), lakhs (lakh = 100,000). In 2,456: 2 is in the thousands, 4 in hundreds, 5 in tens, 6 in ones.

example.problem: The farmer says he has 2,456 kg of rice. Write this in expanded form.
example.solution: 2,456 = 2 thousands + 4 hundreds + 5 tens + 6 ones = 2,000 + 400 + 50 + 6

slides.inSimpleWords: Each digit in a number has a place — ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. The place tells us what value that digit really has.

slides.title: Reading Numbers in Words
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Amir how villagers speak numbers aloud. '2,456 is "Two thousand, four hundred fifty-six," but we say it differently in Hindi — 'do hazaar, char sau, pachpan'.'

points.label: Speaking Numbers
points.text: Write each group of digits (thousands, hundreds, tens, ones) in words. 5,307 is 'five thousand, three hundred seven.'

example.problem: Write 7,842 in words.
example.solution: Seven thousand, eight hundred forty-two.

slides.inSimpleWords: To read a big number out loud, say each group (thousands, hundreds, then tens and ones) in order.

slides.title: Comparing Numbers
slides.storyContext: Two vegetable sellers at the market boast about their sales. One sold 3,456 kg of tomatoes, the other sold 3,546 kg. 'Who sold more?' asks Meera. Amir looks at the first digits — both are 3. Then he checks the second digit: 4 vs. 5. '3,546 is bigger!'

points.label: Comparing Step-by-Step
points.text: Start from the leftmost digit (thousands). If they're the same, move right to hundreds. Keep going until you find different digits — the bigger digit means the bigger number.

example.problem: Compare 6,234 and 6,243. Which is bigger?
example.solution: Both start with 6. Hundreds: both 2. Tens: 3 vs. 4. So 6,243 > 6,234.

slides.inSimpleWords: To compare numbers, line up digits by place. Compare the leftmost first, then move right until you find the difference.

slides.title: Ordering Numbers
slides.storyContext: Dadaji asks them to write the prices of five items in order from cheapest to most expensive: 1,250 rupees (almanac), 890 (oil lamp), 2,100 (lantern), 1,100 (rope), 950 (salt). Meera arranges them: 890, 950, 1,100, 1,250, 2,100.

points.label: Ascending and Descending Order
points.text: Ascending = smallest to largest. Descending = largest to smallest. Compare step-by-step using place values.

example.problem: Order these from smallest to largest: 3,456; 2,100; 3,465; 2,999.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sort numbers by comparing thousands first, then hundreds, tens, and ones.

slides.title: Rounding Numbers
slides.storyContext: At the market, Meera learns that traders often round prices. A vendor says: 'These mangoes cost 1,249 rupees — I'll say 1,250 for simplicity.' Amir asks, 'Why round up?'

points.label: Rounding Rules
points.text: To round to the nearest ten: look at the ones digit. If ≥ 5, round up. If < 5, round down. To round to the nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. Same rule applies.

example.problem: Round 1,249 to the nearest 10 and nearest 100.
example.solution: Nearest 10: ones digit is 9 (≥5), so round up to 1,250. Nearest 100: tens digit is 4 (<5), so round down to 1,200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rounding makes numbers simpler. If the last digit is 5 or more, go up. Less than 5, stay down.

slides.title: The Market Bill
slides.storyContext: Meera and Amir collect their purchases. The shopkeeper writes the bill: Rice 2,456 kg @ 45 rupees/kg, Dal 340 kg, Oil 125 litres, Salt 250 kg. They need to check the total.

example.problem: The shopkeeper's bill shows: Rice (2 items): 1,200 + 856 rupees; Dal: 680 rupees; Oil: 450 rupees; Salt: 125 rupees. What is the total? Also express 1,200 + 856 in expanded form.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use place value to add large numbers step by step — ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Harvest Count
slides.storyContext: Dadaji gives them a final challenge before they leave the market: Three farmers compare harvests. Farmer A grew 5,234 kg of wheat. Farmer B grew 5,243 kg. Farmer C grew 4,999 kg. Meera writes them down and Amir orders them. Can you?

example.problem: Order these harvests from largest to smallest: 5,234; 5,243; 4,999. Also, round 5,243 to the nearest 100.
example.solution: Largest to smallest: 5,243 → 5,234 → 4,999. Rounding 5,243 to nearest 100: tens digit is 4 (<5), so round down to 5,200.

slides.inSimpleWords: Compare by looking at the leftmost different digits. When rounding, check the digit to the right of the place you're rounding to.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Back home, Dadaji listens as Amir and Meera recount their journey. Meera says: 'Numbers were with us every step — in prices, distances, harvests.'

points.text: Numbers have place values: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs.
We can read numbers in words by saying each group aloud.
To compare numbers, look at the leftmost digit first. If equal, move to the next place value.
Ordering means arranging numbers from smallest to largest (or vice versa).
Rounding simplifies numbers: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 rounds down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Place value is the foundation of reading, comparing, and using numbers in daily life.

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir and Meera's Return: Addition and Subtraction on the Road
hook: On the way back, Meera and Amir encounter problems that only addition and subtraction can solve.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: curious older cousin from the city

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: village girl who loves patterns and numbers

characters.name: Dadaji
characters.role: wise grandfather, keeper of stories

slides.title: We the Travellers - II
slides.storyContext: Amir and Meera leave the market with heavy bags of provisions. On the way back, they face challenges: the bridge ahead is damaged, and they must travel through side villages instead. They need to calculate distances, add supplies, and subtract expenses.

slides.title: The Detour
slides.storyContext: The main road is blocked. Meera pulls out Dadaji's old map showing three alternative routes: through the mango orchards (4 km), past the rice paddies (5 km), or along the river (6 km). To reach home, they must add and subtract distances.
slides.inSimpleWords: On their journey, Amir and Meera must solve real problems using addition and subtraction — just like we use math in daily life.

slides.title: Addition with Large Numbers
slides.storyContext: Amir counts: 'From home to market, I walked 1,234 steps. Then from market to the vendor's stall, another 567 steps. How many total steps did I take to reach the vendors?' Meera sets up the addition on paper.

points.label: Column Addition (Place Value Method)
points.text: Write numbers one below the other, aligning by place value (ones below ones, tens below tens, etc.). Add each column from right to left. Carry the tens to the next column if a sum reaches 10 or more.

example.solution:
1234
+  567
------
  1801
Ones: 4+7=11 (write 1, carry 1). Tens: 3+6+1=10 (write 0, carry 1). Hundreds: 2+5+1=8. Thousands: 1. Answer: 1,801.

slides.inSimpleWords: To add large numbers, line them up by place value and add each column from right to left. If a column adds to 10 or more, carry the tens to the next column.

slides.title: Subtraction with Large Numbers
slides.storyContext: They started the journey with 5,000 rupees given by Dadaji. After buying provisions (cost: 3,311 rupees), Meera calculates: 'How much money is left?' Amir sets up the subtraction.

points.label: Column Subtraction (Borrowing)
points.text: Write the larger number on top, smaller below, aligned by place value. Subtract column by column from right to left. If the top digit is smaller than the bottom, borrow 10 from the next place and add it to the current digit.

example.problem: Subtract 5,000 - 3,311.
example.solution:
5000
- 3311
------
  1689
Ones: 0 < 1, borrow from tens. Tens becomes 0-1=-1 (borrow again). Hundreds becomes 9 (after borrowing), 9-3=6. Tens: 9-1=8. Thousands: 4-3=1. Answer: 1,689 rupees left.

slides.inSimpleWords: When the top digit is smaller than the one below, borrow 10 from the next place to the left.

slides.title: Adding Three or More Numbers
slides.storyContext: Along the detoured route, they pass three villages. Meera notes the prices of water pots at each: Village 1: 245 rupees, Village 2: 389 rupees, Village 3: 156 rupees. What's the total cost if they buy from all three?

points.label: Multi-Number Addition
points.text: Align all numbers by place value. Add column by column from right to left, carrying as needed. You can also add two at a time, then add the result to the next number.

example.solution:
245
  389
+ 156
------
  790
Ones: 5+9+6=20 (write 0, carry 2). Tens: 4+8+5+2=19 (write 9, carry 1). Hundreds: 2+3+1+1=7. Answer: 790 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding multiple numbers is like adding two at a time — just keep carrying and adding each column.

slides.title: Checking Addition and Subtraction
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to check if her addition of 245 + 389 + 156 = 790 is correct. She uses the reverse: 790 - 245 - 389 should equal 156. Amir asks, 'How does that help?' 'If the answer is 156, I was right!'

points.label: Verification Methods
points.text: To check addition: use subtraction in reverse. Subtract one addend from the sum; if you get the other addend, you're correct. To check subtraction: add the result to the number you subtracted; you should get the original number.

example.solution:
1689
+ 3311
------
  5000
If the result is 5,000, the subtraction is correct. It is, so our answer was right!

slides.inSimpleWords: To check subtraction, add the answer back to the number you subtracted. You should get the original number.

slides.title: Real-World Problem Solving
slides.storyContext: Dadaji sends word: 'A monsoon flood damaged 2,345 bales of hay from the northern field. The southern field has 4,789 bales. How many bales can still be used?' Meera sets up: 4,789 - 2,345.

points.label: Reading Word Problems
points.text: Identify what you know (the numbers) and what you're asked to find. Decide: is it addition or subtraction? 'How many more' or 'How many left' hints at subtraction. 'How many altogether' hints at addition.

example.problem: The northern field had 2,345 damaged bales. The southern field has 4,789 bales. How many bales can still be used from both fields?
example.solution: Damaged: 2,345. Usable from north: need this info (not given). Usable from south: 4,789. If the question is just about the south, answer is 4,789. If both, we need the northern total before damage.

slides.inSimpleWords: In word problems, find the numbers and decide: Do I add everything together, or subtract what's gone or used?

slides.title: The Journey Totals
slides.storyContext: By evening, Amir tallies the day: They walked 4 km through orchards, 5 km past rice paddies, and 3 km along the river (total distance). They spent 245 rupees on water, 156 on food, and 89 on rope. Meera adds up the distances, then subtracts the expenses from their remaining money.

example.problem: Distance: 4 + 5 + 3 = ? km. Expenses: 245 + 156 + 89 = ? rupees. If they had 1,689 rupees left, how much remains after these expenses?
example.solution: Distance: 4 + 5 + 3 = 12 km. Expenses: 245 + 156 + 89 = 490 rupees. Remaining: 1,689 - 490 = 1,199 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break multi-step problems into pieces: add the distances, add the expenses, then subtract.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Final Stretch
slides.storyContext: Dadaji asks one last puzzle before they rest: 'The journey from market to home is 12 km total. They've walked 4 km through orchards and 5 km past paddies. How many km remain? And if they spent 490 rupees already and have 1,199 rupees left, how much did Meera have to start this leg of the journey?'

example.problem: Distance walked: 4 + 5 = 9 km. Total distance: 12 km. Distance left: 12 - 9 = ? km. Money spent: 490. Money left: 1,199. Starting money for this leg: ?
example.solution: Distance left: 12 - 9 = 3 km. Starting money: 490 + 1,199 = 1,689 rupees.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two-step problems: solve one operation, then use that answer in the next.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Amir and Meera finally reach home. Dadaji listens as they explain how addition and subtraction solved every problem on their journey.

points.text: Addition: Align by place value, add column by column from right to left, carry tens to the next place.
Subtraction: Align by place value, subtract column by column, borrow 10 from the next place if needed.
Check addition with subtraction in reverse; check subtraction by adding the answer back.
Multi-step problems: solve piece by piece, using one answer in the next step.
In real life, 'altogether' signals addition; 'left' or 'remaining' signals subtraction.

slides.inSimpleWords: Addition and subtraction are the tools we use to count what we have, what we spent, and what remains.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Multiplication and Division on the Coconut Farm
hook: Meera helps with the harvest on Dadaji's coconut farm — and learns that grouping and sharing are the heart of multiplication and division.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: practical girl who loves working with her hands

characters.name: Dadaji
characters.role: wise grandfather who teaches through farm work

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: farm worker, patient with numbers

slides.title: Coconut Farm
slides.storyContext: Meera spends the harvest season on Dadaji's coconut farm. Trees are heavy with coconuts. Dadaji asks her to help organize the harvest: group coconuts for sale, divide them fairly among farm workers, and count yields.

slides.title: The Great Coconut Count
slides.storyContext: On the first day, Meera climbs the farm's fence and counts: 'Each of the 6 trees has 12 coconuts. How many coconuts altogether?' Dadaji smiles: 'That's multiplication. You're grouping — 6 groups of 12.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication is when you have equal groups and need to find the total. Division is when you split a total into equal groups.

slides.title: Multiplication as Repeated Addition
slides.storyContext: Meera starts counting: '12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 12.' Ravi interrupts: 'That's 6 twelves. In math, we write 6 × 12.' Meera writes it down and calculates: 6 × 12 = 72 coconuts.

points.label: Understanding Multiplication
points.text: Multiplication is a quick way to add equal groups. 6 × 12 means '6 groups of 12' or '12 added 6 times.' The first number is how many groups; the second is what's in each group.

example.problem: There are 5 baskets. Each basket holds 8 coconuts. How many coconuts total?

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication is grouping. 5 × 8 means 5 groups of 8 each, or 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 8.

slides.title: Multiplication Tables and Facts
slides.storyContext: Meera realizes Dadaji uses a quick method. He doesn't add 12 six times — he just knows 6 × 12 = 72 from memory. Ravi teaches her: 'We learn multiplication tables — quick facts we memorize so we don't have to add each time.'

points.label: Multiplication Facts (2–10 tables)
points.text: Memorize: 2×3=6, 3×3=9, 4×5=20, 5×7=35, 6×8=48, 7×9=63, 8×10=80, etc. Knowing these facts lets you multiply larger numbers using the place-value method (multiply each digit, then add).

example.problem: Use 7 × 8 = 56 to find 7 × 80.

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorized times tables make multiplication fast. 7 × 8 = 56 is a fact you learn and remember.

slides.title: Multiplication with Two-Digit Numbers
slides.storyContext: Later, Dadaji says: 'We have 23 bags of coconuts, each with 15 coconuts. How many total?' Meera panics — 23 × 15 is not in the times table. Ravi shows her the place-value method: break 23 into 20 + 3, and 15 into 10 + 5.

points.label: Column Multiplication (Lattice or Standard)
points.text: Write the numbers vertically. Multiply the ones digit of the bottom number by each digit of the top, writing results below. Then multiply the tens digit of the bottom number by each digit of the top, shifting left one place. Add all rows.

example.problem: Multiply 23 × 15.

slides.inSimpleWords: For two-digit multiplication, multiply by the ones digit, then the tens digit (shifted left), then add.

slides.title: Division and Fair Sharing
slides.storyContext: At day's end, Meera and Ravi sort 72 coconuts into 6 equal piles for the 6 farm workers. Meera divides: 72 ÷ 6. Ravi asks, 'How many does each worker get?' Meera counts: 12 each.

points.label: Division as Sharing
points.text: Division splits a total into equal groups. 72 ÷ 6 means 'divide 72 into 6 equal groups' or 'how many are in each group if 72 is split 6 ways?' The answer is 12.

example.problem: There are 48 coconuts and 8 workers. How many coconuts does each worker get?
example.solution: 48 ÷ 8 = 6. Each worker gets 6 coconuts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Division means fair sharing. 48 ÷ 8 means split 48 into 8 equal piles.

slides.title: Division with Remainders
slides.storyContext: The next day, they have 50 coconuts to pack into baskets holding 6 each. Meera counts: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48 — and 2 left over. Ravi says: '50 ÷ 6 = 8 remainder 2.' Meera writes: 50 ÷ 6 = 8 R 2.

points.label: Understanding Remainders
points.text: Not all divisions work evenly. When 50 is divided by 6, you get 8 full groups of 6 (= 48) with 2 left over. We write this as 'quotient R remainder' or '8 R 2.'

example.problem: Divide 35 coconuts among 4 workers. How many each, and how many are left?
example.solution: 35 ÷ 4 = 8 R 3. Each worker gets 8, and 3 are left over.

slides.inSimpleWords: In division, if there's anything left that doesn't fill a full group, that's the remainder.

slides.title: The Harvest Report
slides.storyContext: End of harvest. Dadaji asks Meera to report: 'We picked 18 baskets, each with 24 coconuts. They go to 3 markets equally. How many to each market? How many baskets per market?'

example.problem: 18 baskets × 24 coconuts per basket = total. Divide total by 3 markets.
example.solution: 18 × 24: (18 × 20) + (18 × 4) = 360 + 72 = 432 total coconuts. 432 ÷ 3 = 144 coconuts per market. For baskets: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 baskets per market.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply to find a total, then divide to share it fairly.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Coconut Challenge
slides.storyContext: Dadaji poses the final puzzle: 'A farmer has 5 coconut trees. Each tree yields 32 coconuts. He sells them in bundles of 8. How many bundles can he make? If 2 bundles spoil, how many good bundles are left?'

example.problem: 5 trees × 32 coconuts = total. Divide by 8 to get bundles. Subtract 2 spoiled bundles.
example.solution: 5 × 32 = 160 coconuts. 160 ÷ 8 = 20 bundles. 20 - 2 = 18 good bundles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multi-step problems: multiply first to find the total, then divide to make groups, then subtract what's lost.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Meera sits with Dadaji at sunset. 'I never thought the harvest involved so much math,' she says. Dadaji smiles: 'Math is everywhere on the farm.'

points.text: Multiplication is grouping: 6 × 12 means 6 groups of 12 each.
Memorize times tables for quick multiplication.
For two-digit multiplication, multiply by ones, then tens (shifted), then add.
Division is fair sharing: 72 ÷ 6 means divide 72 into 6 equal groups.
Remainders are what's left after dividing into equal groups.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiplication finds totals from equal groups. Division splits totals into equal groups.

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Symmetry: Patterns in the Carpet Weaver's Studio
hook: Amir discovers that beautiful carpets and textiles are built on the math of symmetry — mirror images and repeating patterns.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: curious boy fascinated by patterns and design

characters.name: Ustad Kareem
characters.role: master carpet weaver who creates symmetrical designs

characters.name: Sana
characters.role: Ustad's daughter, who helps design patterns

slides.title: Symmetrical Designs
slides.storyContext: Amir visits a carpet weaver's studio in the bazaar. The walls are covered with rolled carpets, each with intricate patterns. Ustad Kareem invites him: 'Want to learn how I design these patterns? It all starts with symmetry.'

slides.title: The Repeating Pattern
slides.storyContext: Ustad shows Amir a half-finished carpet. 'See this line down the middle? If I fold the carpet here, the left side mirrors the right side perfectly. That's symmetry. It's how we make sure every carpet looks balanced and beautiful.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry means one half mirrors the other. A fold line down the middle is called a line of symmetry.

slides.title: Line Symmetry (Mirror Symmetry)
slides.storyContext: Sana draws a simple flower design on paper. She folds it in half and says: 'Look, when I fold here, the petals on both sides match exactly. This fold line is the line of symmetry.' Amir traces the fold line.

points.label: Line Symmetry Definition
points.text: A shape has line symmetry if one half is a mirror image of the other half. The fold line is called the line of symmetry or line of reflection. Some shapes have 1 line of symmetry, some have many, some have none.

example.problem: A heart shape: how many lines of symmetry does it have?
example.solution: A heart has 1 line of symmetry — the vertical line down the middle that divides it into left and right halves that mirror each other.

slides.inSimpleWords: If you can fold a shape so both halves match exactly, that fold line is a line of symmetry.

slides.title: Finding Lines of Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Amir starts to see patterns everywhere. A square has how many lines of symmetry? Sana draws it: a vertical line down the middle, a horizontal line across, and two diagonal lines. 'Four lines total!' says Amir.

points.label: Lines of Symmetry in Common Shapes
points.text: Square: 4 (vertical, horizontal, 2 diagonals). Rectangle: 2 (vertical, horizontal). Circle: infinite (any line through the center). Equilateral triangle: 3. Isosceles triangle: 1.

example.problem: How many lines of symmetry does an equilateral triangle have?
example.solution: An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry: one from each vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count how many ways you can fold a shape so both halves match perfectly.

slides.title: Rotational Symmetry
slides.storyContext: Ustad shows Amir a tile design with a pinwheel pattern. 'If I spin this design 90 degrees, it looks exactly the same. Spin it again, still the same. This is rotational symmetry.' He rotates it to show.

points.label: Rotational Symmetry Definition
points.text: A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks the same after rotating it (turning it) by less than 360 degrees. The number of times it matches is the order of rotational symmetry.

example.problem: A square rotated 90 degrees looks the same. What is its order of rotational symmetry?
example.solution: A square has rotational symmetry of order 4 because it matches itself after rotating 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Rotational symmetry means a shape looks the same after spinning it. The number of times it matches is its order.

slides.title: Symmetry in Nature and Design
slides.storyContext: Sana points out symmetries in the studio: 'Look at butterflies, flowers, snowflakes, even our faces — most things in nature are symmetrical. Ustad uses this to design carpets that please the eye.'

points.label: Real-World Symmetry
points.text: Butterflies: bilateral (left-right mirror). Flowers: radial (multiple lines through center). Snowflakes: 6-fold rotational. Indian rangoli patterns: both line and rotational symmetry.

example.problem: A butterfly has how many lines of symmetry?
example.solution: A butterfly typically has 1 line of symmetry (down the middle), making it bilaterally symmetrical.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most living things and pretty designs use symmetry because it looks balanced and beautiful.

slides.title: Repeating Patterns (Tessellation)
slides.storyContext: Ustad unrolls a carpet with a pattern that repeats over and over — the same flower motif appearing in rows. 'This is a tessellation,' he explains. 'The pattern tiles repeat without gaps or overlaps, covering the whole carpet.'

points.label: Tessellations and Patterns
points.text: A tessellation is a repeating pattern that covers a surface with no gaps or overlaps. Squares, rectangles, and hexagons tessellate perfectly. Triangles and some other shapes also tessellate.

example.problem: A tile in the shape of a regular hexagon can tessellate. Why?
example.solution: Regular hexagons fit together perfectly with angles of 120° at each corner. Six hexagons meet at a point (6 × 120° = 720° > 360°, but they fit around a center), creating a honeycomb pattern with no gaps.

slides.inSimpleWords: Some shapes fit together perfectly to cover a surface with no gaps — like floor tiles or honeycomb.

slides.title: Designing a Symmetrical Carpet
slides.storyContext: Ustad challenges Amir: 'Design half a carpet border for me. Make it symmetrical with a vertical line of symmetry down the middle. Then I'll mirror it to complete the design.' Amir sketches a border with flowers and geometric shapes.

example.problem: If the left half of a carpet border has a pattern with 4 flowers, and the right half mirrors it (same positions), how many flowers total?
example.solution: Left half: 4 flowers. Right half (mirror): 4 flowers. Total: 4 + 4 = 8 flowers. (In practice, the central flower on the line of symmetry is shared, so: 3 left-only + 1 center + 3 right-only = 7 unique positions, but 8 flower images if the center is counted twice in the fold-open design.)

slides.inSimpleWords: To create a symmetrical design, draw one half beautifully, then mirror it to complete.

slides.title: Your Turn: Symmetry Hunt
slides.storyContext: Ustad gives Amir a task: 'Walk around the studio and find 5 objects or patterns with symmetry. For each, tell me: does it have line symmetry, rotational symmetry, or both? How many lines? What's the order?'

example.problem: A decorative plate with a star pattern: Line or rotational symmetry (or both)? How many lines of symmetry? Order of rotational symmetry?
example.solution: A 5-pointed star: 5 lines of symmetry (from each point to the center). Rotational symmetry of order 5 (72° rotations). It has both.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look for symmetry in everyday objects. Every carpet, tile, and flower reveals the math of balance.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Amir leaves the studio with a sketch Ustad gave him — a perfectly symmetrical design. 'Math isn't just numbers,' Ustad says. 'It's also beauty, patterns, and balance.'

points.text: Line symmetry: one half mirrors the other across a fold line.
Different shapes have different numbers of lines of symmetry (square: 4, circle: infinite).
Rotational symmetry: a shape looks the same after spinning it by less than 360°.
Tessellations are repeating patterns with no gaps or overlaps.
Symmetry appears in nature (butterflies, flowers, snowflakes) and human design (carpets, tiles, architecture).

slides.inSimpleWords: Symmetry is the math of balance and beauty — it's everywhere in nature and design.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera Measures: Fractions and Area on the Quilt
hook: Grandmother's quilt is made of colorful patches, and Meera discovers that fractions and area are woven into every square.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: practical girl who helps her grandmother

characters.name: Grandmother
characters.role: patient elder who weaves stories into cloth

characters.name: Dadi
characters.role: also grandmother, Meera's other grandparent

slides.title: Grandmother's Quilt
slides.storyContext: On a cool evening, Meera sits with her grandmother, who is making a quilt from fabric scraps. 'Each piece is a memory,' Grandmother says, showing Meera patches of old saris and turbans. 'And math lives in every measurement.'

slides.title: Cutting the Cloth
slides.storyContext: Grandmother shows Meera how to cut a large piece of fabric into smaller patches. 'This big cloth is one whole. I'll divide it into smaller pieces — halves, quarters, thirds. Each piece is a fraction of the whole.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction is a part of a whole. Half means 1 out of 2 equal parts. Quarter means 1 out of 4 equal parts.

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Grandmother cuts a square patch into 4 equal pieces. 'Each piece is 1/4 of the whole. Two pieces together are 2/4, which is the same as 1/2.' Meera counts: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 (the whole).

points.label: Fraction Notation
points.text: A fraction has two numbers: numerator (top) and denominator (bottom). The denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is divided into. The numerator tells you how many parts you have. 1/4 means 1 part out of 4.

example.problem: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. Meera eats 3 slices. What fraction does she eat? What fraction remains?
example.solution: Eaten: 3/8. Remaining: 5/8 (since 8 - 3 = 5, and 5/8 + 3/8 = 8/8 = 1 whole pizza).

slides.inSimpleWords: The numerator is 'how many,' the denominator is 'how many equal parts total.' 3/8 means 3 out of 8 equal parts.

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges patches: 2/4 of the quilt is red fabric. Grandmother says: 'But 2/4 is the same as 1/2. Two quarters equal one half. They're equivalent.' Meera folds a square in half and into quarters to see.

points.label: Equivalent Fractions
points.text: Different fractions can represent the same part. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. Multiply or divide both numerator and denominator by the same number to find equivalent fractions.

example.problem: Is 3/6 the same as 1/2?

slides.inSimpleWords: 1/2, 2/4, 3/6, 4/8 all show the same amount — half of the whole.

slides.title: Comparing Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to place patches in order: 1/2 of blue, 1/4 of green, 3/4 of yellow. 'Which color has the most fabric?' Grandmother teaches: 'Compare by finding a common denominator or by looking at the size.'

points.label: Comparing Fractions
points.text: If denominators are the same, compare numerators: 3/4 > 2/4. If numerators are the same, the smaller denominator is bigger: 1/2 > 1/4. Use equivalent fractions to compare with different denominators.

example.problem: Which is bigger: 1/2 or 1/4?
example.solution: Both have numerator 1. The smaller denominator (2) means bigger pieces, so 1/2 > 1/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: When comparing fractions with the same denominator, the bigger numerator wins. When the numerator is the same, the smaller denominator wins.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Grandmother combines patches: 'I have 1/4 red and 2/4 blue. Together, that's 3/4 of the quilt.' Meera writes: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. 'What if I remove 1/4 red?' '3/4 - 1/4 = 2/4, which is 1/2.'

points.label: Adding/Subtracting with Same Denominator
points.text: If denominators are the same, add or subtract numerators. Keep the denominator: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. If denominators differ, find a common denominator first.

example.solution: Convert to common denominator: 1/2 = 2/4. Now 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: To add fractions with the same denominator, add the numerators. To add with different denominators, convert to a common denominator first.

slides.title: Area and Square Units
slides.storyContext: Grandmother measures patches with a ruler. 'This square patch is 4 cm on each side. Its area is 4 × 4 = 16 square centimeters, or 16 cm².' Meera traces a square grid on paper to understand.

points.label: Area of Rectangles and Squares
points.text: Area = length × width (measured in square units: cm², m², etc.). For a square, area = side × side.

example.problem: A rectangular patch is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. What is its area?
example.solution: Area = 6 × 4 = 24 square centimeters (24 cm²).

slides.inSimpleWords: Area is how much space a flat shape covers. Multiply length times width for a rectangle.

slides.title: The Quilt Assembly
slides.storyContext: Grandmother plans the quilt: '4 patches of red (each 1/4 of the quilt), 4 patches of blue (each 1/4), and 4 patches of yellow (each 1/4). That's 12 patches total, each 20 cm × 20 cm.' Meera calculates the area of the whole quilt.

example.problem: 12 patches, each 20 cm × 20 cm. What is the total area? Also, what fraction is red?
example.solution: Area per patch: 20 × 20 = 400 cm². Total area: 12 × 400 = 4,800 cm². Red patches: 4 out of 12 = 4/12 = 1/3 of the quilt.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions and area combine: each patch is 1/12 of the quilt, and its area contributes to the total.

slides.title: Your Turn: Design Your Quilt
slides.storyContext: Grandmother asks Meera to design a small quilt: '12 patches total. Make 1/2 red, 1/3 blue, and 1/6 yellow. If each patch is 15 cm × 15 cm, what's the total area? How many of each color?'

example.problem: Design a 12-patch quilt: 1/2 red, 1/3 blue, 1/6 yellow. Count patches of each color. Find total area if each patch is 15 × 15 cm.
example.solution: Red: 1/2 × 12 = 6 patches. Blue: 1/3 × 12 = 4 patches. Yellow: 1/6 × 12 = 2 patches. (Total: 6+4+2=12.) Area per patch: 15×15=225 cm². Total area: 12×225=2,700 cm².

slides.inSimpleWords: To find a fraction of a whole, multiply the fraction by the total.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: The quilt is complete. Grandmother wraps it around Meera's shoulders. 'You stitched this quilt with your own hands, and you measured it with your mind. Math and art go together.'

points.text: Fractions represent parts of a whole. The numerator says 'how many,' the denominator says 'how many parts total.'
Equivalent fractions represent the same amount: 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6.
Compare fractions by finding common denominators or by understanding relative sizes.
Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator by adding/subtracting numerators.
Area = length × width. The total area of a quilt is the sum of all patch areas.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are parts. Area is space. Together, they help us measure and create.

subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Race: Time and Speed
hook: Amir enters a village race, and discovers that time, distance, and speed are connected by math.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: competitive boy who loves racing

characters.name: Coach Raj
characters.role: village sports trainer, uses math to teach running

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: Amir's cousin, keeps track of times

slides.title: Racing Seconds
slides.storyContext: The village announces a 400-meter race. Amir trains with Coach Raj, who explains: 'To win, you need to run 400 meters in the shortest time. But time and speed are connected — understanding this math will help you run faster.'

slides.title: Training Day
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj times Amir running 100 meters: 20 seconds. 'Good!' says Coach. 'Now I'll teach you about speed. Speed is distance divided by time. You ran 100 meters in 20 seconds, so your speed is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 meters per second.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Speed tells you how fast something moves. It's distance traveled divided by time taken. If you run 100 meters in 20 seconds, your speed is 5 meters per second.

slides.title: Understanding Time: Seconds, Minutes, Hours
slides.storyContext: Meera keeps a stopwatch. 'One minute is 60 seconds,' she explains. 'One hour is 60 minutes, so 3,600 seconds.' Amir practices: 20 seconds, 45 seconds, 1 minute 15 seconds (= 75 seconds).

points.label: Time Conversions
points.text: 60 seconds = 1 minute. 60 minutes = 1 hour. 1 hour = 3,600 seconds. To convert: multiply to go to smaller units (minutes to seconds), divide to go to larger units (seconds to minutes).

example.problem: Convert 2 minutes 30 seconds to just seconds. Convert 180 seconds to minutes.
example.solution: 2 min 30 sec = (2 × 60) + 30 = 120 + 30 = 150 seconds. 180 seconds ÷ 60 = 3 minutes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply by 60 to convert minutes to seconds. Divide by 60 to convert seconds to minutes.

slides.title: Measuring Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj marks the track: '100 meters is about the length of the main street. 400 meters is one lap around our field. 1 kilometer is 1,000 meters — that's the distance from the village to the neighboring town.'

points.label: Distance Units
points.text: 1 kilometer (km) = 1,000 meters (m). 1 meter (m) = 100 centimeters (cm). In a race, we measure distances in meters and kilometers.

example.problem: A race is 2 kilometers long. How many meters?

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 km = 1,000 m. Use this conversion to switch between kilometers and meters.

slides.title: Speed = Distance ÷ Time
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj teaches the formula. 'Speed equals distance divided by time. If Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, his speed is 400 ÷ 80 = 5 meters per second.' Amir practices: 100 m in 20 sec → 5 m/s. 200 m in 50 sec → 4 m/s.

points.label: Speed Formula
points.text: Speed = Distance ÷ Time. If speed is S, distance is D, and time is T, then S = D ÷ T. Units: meters per second (m/s), kilometers per hour (km/h), etc.

example.problem: A runner covers 200 meters in 40 seconds. What is the speed?
example.solution: Speed = 200 m ÷ 40 s = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed = how far ÷ how long. A runner who covers 100 m in 20 s has a speed of 5 m per second.

slides.title: Rearranging the Formula: Finding Time or Distance
slides.storyContext: Coach challenges Amir differently: 'If you want to run 400 meters at 5 m/s, how long will it take?' Amir rearranges: Time = Distance ÷ Speed = 400 ÷ 5 = 80 seconds. Later: 'If you have 60 seconds and want to run at 6 m/s, how far will you go?' Distance = Speed × Time = 6 × 60 = 360 meters.

points.label: Rearranging Speed Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time, or D = S × T. Time = Distance ÷ Speed, or T = D ÷ S.

example.problem: Amir runs at 5 m/s. How far does he run in 25 seconds? How long to run 500 meters?
example.solution: Distance: 5 × 25 = 125 meters. Time: 500 ÷ 5 = 100 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed × Time = Distance. Distance ÷ Speed = Time. Distance ÷ Time = Speed. Know any two, find the third.

slides.title: Comparing Speeds
slides.storyContext: Two runners compete: Amir (400 m in 80 s) and his friend Ravi (400 m in 100 s). Meera calculates: Amir's speed = 400 ÷ 80 = 5 m/s. Ravi's speed = 400 ÷ 100 = 4 m/s. 'Amir is faster!'

points.label: Comparing Speeds
points.text: Calculate speed for each runner or vehicle. The higher speed means faster movement. Use the same units to compare fairly.

example.problem: Runner A: 200 m in 40 s. Runner B: 300 m in 60 s. Who is faster?
example.solution: Runner A speed: 200 ÷ 40 = 5 m/s. Runner B speed: 300 ÷ 60 = 5 m/s. Same speed! It's a tie.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each runner's speed, then compare. Bigger speed = faster runner.

slides.title: The Big Race Day
slides.storyContext: Race day arrives. Amir runs 400 meters in 80 seconds, averaging 5 m/s. Ravi takes 100 seconds (4 m/s). A cyclist passes them both, covering 600 meters in 60 seconds (10 m/s). Meera records all speeds and times.

example.problem: In the race: Amir (400 m, 80 s), Ravi (400 m, 100 s), Cyclist (600 m, 60 s). Find each one's speed. Who is fastest? If the cyclist had run 1 hour at that speed, how far would go?
example.solution: Amir: 5 m/s. Ravi: 4 m/s. Cyclist: 10 m/s. Cyclist is fastest. In 1 hour (3,600 s): 10 × 3,600 = 36,000 meters = 36 km.

slides.inSimpleWords: Calculate each speed, compare, and use speed to predict distance over longer times.

slides.title: Your Turn: Plan the Training
slides.storyContext: Coach Raj asks Amir: 'If you improve to 6 m/s for the 400-meter race, what will your time be? And if I want you to run 1 kilometer at 5 m/s, how many seconds will that take?'

example.problem: At 6 m/s for 400 m, find time. At 5 m/s for 1 km (1,000 m), find time.
example.solution: Time for 400 m at 6 m/s: 400 ÷ 6 ≈ 66.7 seconds. Time for 1,000 m at 5 m/s: 1,000 ÷ 5 = 200 seconds = 3 minutes 20 seconds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use Time = Distance ÷ Speed to find how long a run takes.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: After the race, Amir sits with Coach Raj. 'I never knew math was the key to running fast,' Amir says. Coach smiles: 'Everything has math in it — racing, cooking, building, traveling.'

points.text: Time conversions: 60 seconds = 1 minute, 60 minutes = 1 hour.
Distance units: 1 km = 1,000 m. Measure distance in meters and kilometers.
Speed = Distance ÷ Time. A runner's speed is how far they go per unit time.
Distance = Speed × Time. Time = Distance ÷ Speed. Use these formulas to solve problems.
Compare speeds by calculating each one and seeing which is larger.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed, distance, and time are connected. Know any two, and you can find the third.

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Animal Jumps: Data, Graphs, and Measurement
hook: Meera studies how far different animals can jump and organizes the data into tables and graphs.

characters.name: Meera
characters.role: curious scientist who loves animals and collecting data

characters.name: Grandfather
characters.role: patient elder with encyclopedic knowledge of village animals

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: Meera's cousin, helps organize data

slides.title: Animal Jumps
slides.storyContext: Meera watches rabbits, frogs, grasshoppers, and dogs jumping in the village courtyard. 'How far can each one jump?' she wonders. She decides to measure and collect data to find out.

slides.title: Collecting Measurements
slides.storyContext: Meera marks a starting line with chalk and measures how far each animal jumps using a meter stick. Amir writes down the numbers: Rabbit 1: 2 m, Rabbit 2: 1.8 m, Frog 1: 0.6 m, Frog 2: 0.7 m, Grasshopper 1: 0.5 m, Grasshopper 2: 0.4 m, Dog 1: 1.5 m, Dog 2: 1.2 m. 'Now we organize this data,' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect by measuring or observing. We organize data into tables to see patterns.

slides.title: Measuring in Meters and Centimeters
slides.storyContext: Meera's rabbit jumps 2 meters. Another jumps 1 meter 80 centimeters (1.8 m). Grandfather explains: '1 meter = 100 centimeters. So 1 meter 80 centimeters is 180 centimeters total, or 1.8 meters.'

points.label: Meter-Centimeter Conversion
points.text: 1 meter = 100 centimeters. To convert meters to centimeters, multiply by 100. To convert centimeters to meters, divide by 100.

example.problem: A frog jumps 65 centimeters. Express this in meters.
example.solution: 65 cm ÷ 100 = 0.65 meters (or 65 cm = 0 m 65 cm).

slides.inSimpleWords: 1 meter = 100 cm. 1.5 meters = 150 cm. 80 cm = 0.8 meters.

slides.title: Creating a Data Table
slides.storyContext: Meera organizes the jump data into a clear table: Animal type, Number of jumps recorded, Average jump distance. Rabbit: 2, 1.9 m. Frog: 2, 0.65 m. Grasshopper: 2, 0.45 m. Dog: 2, 1.35 m. 'Now we can see which animal jumps farthest!'

points.label: Organizing Data in Tables
points.text: A table lists data in rows and columns. Rows are categories (animal type). Columns are measurements (distance, frequency, etc.). This makes it easy to compare and analyze.

example.problem: Create a table for: Rabbit 2 m, 1.8 m; Frog 0.6 m, 0.7 m. Calculate averages.
example.solution: Rabbit average: (2 + 1.8) ÷ 2 = 1.9 m. Frog average: (0.6 + 0.7) ÷ 2 = 0.65 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: A table organizes data so you can see patterns. Rows and columns make data easy to read and compare.

slides.title: Calculating Averages (Mean)
slides.storyContext: Meera has three grasshopper jump measurements: 0.5 m, 0.4 m, and 0.6 m. 'What's the average jump?' Amir adds: 0.5 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.5 m. Then divides by 3: 1.5 ÷ 3 = 0.5 m average.

points.label: Calculating the Mean (Average)
points.text: Add all the values, then divide by how many values there are. Average = (sum of all values) ÷ (number of values).

example.problem: Dog jumps: 1.5 m, 1.2 m, 1.4 m. What is the average?

slides.inSimpleWords: Average = sum of all values ÷ number of values. It tells you the typical value in a set.

slides.title: Creating a Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar graph on graph paper. The x-axis lists animals (Rabbit, Frog, Grasshopper, Dog). The y-axis shows distance in meters (0 to 2 m). She draws bars for each animal's average jump. The rabbit bar is tallest, the grasshopper bar shortest.

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: A bar graph uses rectangular bars to show data. The height of each bar represents a value. Bar graphs make it easy to compare values at a glance.

example.problem: Draw a bar graph for: Rabbit 1.9 m, Frog 0.65 m, Grasshopper 0.45 m, Dog 1.35 m.
example.solution: Create axes. X-axis: animal names. Y-axis: distance (0-2 m). Draw bars: Rabbit tallest, then Dog, then Frog, then Grasshopper.

slides.inSimpleWords: In a bar graph, taller bars mean bigger values. You can compare all values at once by looking at bar heights.

slides.title: Reading and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Looking at the bar graph, Meera asks: 'Which animal jumps the farthest? How much farther does a rabbit jump than a frog?' Amir reads: 'Rabbit jumps 1.9 m, frog jumps 0.65 m. Difference: 1.9 - 0.65 = 1.25 m.'

points.label: Analyzing Graphs
points.text: Read the axes carefully. Compare bar heights. Calculate differences and ratios if needed. Look for trends (is data increasing, decreasing, or stable?).

example.problem: From the bar graph: How much farther does a dog jump than a grasshopper?
example.solution: Dog: 1.35 m. Grasshopper: 0.45 m. Difference: 1.35 - 0.45 = 0.9 m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read a graph by looking at the axes and comparing bar heights. You can calculate differences between values.

slides.title: The Complete Study
slides.storyContext: Meera writes a report: 'I measured jump distances for 4 animals. Rabbits jump the farthest (average 1.9 m), followed by dogs (1.35 m), frogs (0.65 m), and grasshoppers (0.45 m). I organized the data in a table and created a bar graph to show the comparison.'

example.problem: Create a full report: table, average calculations, and graph interpretation.
example.solution:
Table:
Animal | Jump 1 | Jump 2 | Average
Rabbit | 2.0 | 1.8 | 1.9
Frog | 0.6 | 0.7 | 0.65
Grasshopper | 0.5 | 0.4 | 0.45
Dog | 1.5 | 1.2 | 1.35

Interpretation: Rabbit jumps farthest; grasshopper jumps shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: A complete data analysis includes measurements, a table, averages, a graph, and conclusions.

slides.title: Your Turn: Analyze More Animals
slides.storyContext: Grandfather asks Meera: 'If a cat jumps 1.1 m and 1.3 m, what's its average? Where does it fit in your graph? Which animals jump twice as far as a grasshopper?'

example.problem: Cat jumps: 1.1 m, 1.3 m. Find average. Is it more or less than a dog's average (1.35 m)? Which animal jumps about 2× a grasshopper's distance (0.45 m)?
example.solution: Cat average: (1.1 + 1.3) ÷ 2 = 1.2 m. Less than dog's 1.35 m. 2 × grasshopper: 2 × 0.45 = 0.9 m ≈ dog's distance (1.35 m is close, but not exactly 2×; frog at 0.65 m is not 2×; rabbit at 1.9 m is 4.2×).

slides.inSimpleWords: Use averages and graphs to compare new data with existing data. Look for patterns and multiples.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: Meera displays her poster with the data, graph, and conclusions at the village school fair. Grandfather smiles: 'You've learned to collect data, organize it, and tell a story with numbers and graphs.'

points.text: Measurement: use meters and centimeters; 1 m = 100 cm.
Data tables organize information in rows and columns for easy comparison.
Average (mean) = sum of values ÷ number of values. It represents a typical value.
Bar graphs use bar height to show values visually. Easy to compare at a glance.
Read graphs by checking axes, comparing heights, and calculating differences.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data, tables, and graphs help us understand the world. Measurements, organization, and analysis tell stories.
